summary: Proposes a client-side image map extension to HTML, so that clickable regions of an image are defined in the page itself rather than on the server. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 2854.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking a faraway computer which part of a picture you clicked, the page already knows what each part does.

subtitle: Clickable image regions defined by the page, not the server.

tldr.problem: In the early web, image maps required a server request to determine where a user clicked on an image. This added latency and only worked over HTTP, and there was no way for browsers to show where each region leads before clicking.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1980 proposes the USEMAP attribute and MAP element, allowing the browser to store a map of clickable regions with their destinations in the same document. The browser matches clicks to regions locally and navigates directly.
tldr.outcome: Client-side image maps became widely supported and eventually replaced server-side maps. This RFC is now historic, superseded by RFC 2854 (HTML 4.01).

today: RFC 1980 is now Historic and was superseded by RFC 2854 (HTML 4.01). Client-side image maps are still part of HTML, but interactive elements and CSS have since become the preferred way to create clickable regions on images.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Client-side image maps let a page define clickable regions within an image directly in the HTML. Each region has a shape, coordinates, and a destination URL. When the user clicks the image, the browser determines which region was clicked and navigates to the corresponding link.

The earlier approach, server-side image maps, required every click to be sent to a server script, which would then decide where to navigate. This had three main problems: it only worked over HTTP, clicks were slower (a server round-trip for each one), and browsers could not show users where regions led before clicking.
sections.plainLanguage: Image maps let you click different parts of a picture to go to different places, like a treasure map. Client-side means the page tells your browser which parts go where, instead of asking the server each time.

sections.title: Map Syntax and Elements
sections.content:
A MAP element wraps one or more AREA elements. Each AREA specifies a region with a SHAPE (RECT, CIRCLE, or POLYGON), COORDS (pixel coordinates), an optional HREF (destination), and an optional ALT text for non-graphical browsers.

Rectangular regions use left,top,right,bottom coordinates. Circular regions use center_x,center_y,radius. Polygonal regions list vertices as x1,y1,x2,y2,...,xn,yn. An IMG element references a map with the USEMAP attribute, optionally followed by the map name (or a URI and fragment if the map is in another file). The first matching region takes precedence when regions overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: You draw rectangles, circles, or shapes on an image, give each one a link, and give the map a name. When someone clicks, the browser checks which shape was hit and goes to that link.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility
sections.content:
The proposal includes three fallback mechanisms for browsers that do not support client-side maps. First, an image can have both USEMAP and ISMAP attributes, so it works with either implementation. Second, wrapping the image in an anchor tag (A element) makes clicks go to a default destination. Third, an image with no USEMAP or ISMAP and not in an anchor simply does not act as a link.

Browsers ignore unknown attributes and elements, so older browsers safely ignore USEMAP and MAP without breaking.
sections.plainLanguage: If your browser does not understand client-side maps, the page can fall back to a server-side map or just a plain link. Everyone's browser can handle it somehow.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that clicking a region may cause a URI to be dereferenced, just as with a normal link. The same security considerations that apply to URLs apply here: users should be aware of what URL they are about to visit, and servers should validate data received from form submissions. No new security hazards are introduced beyond those of standard hyperlinks.
sections.plainLanguage: When you click, you go to a URL like any link, so the same safety rules apply. Make sure you trust where the link goes.
